R_H1.passageTitle: Four days on the Milford Track

passages.label: A
passages.text: On a map, the Milford Track starts near a lake and ends near the sea. Between the two points, walkers cross some of the most famous scenery on New Zealand's South Island. The route is 53.5 kilometres. In the Great Walks season, this popular walk takes four days. Walkers spend three nights in huts. A local library may have an international guide to the national park.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Day one begins with a boat trip from Te Anau Downs to Glade Wharf. The walk to Clinton Hut is only five kilometres and usually takes between one hour and one and a half hours. The path goes through beech forest beside the Clinton River. Every walker spends the first night at Clinton Hut. The river stays by the path through this part of the walk. People have time to get off the boat and find the path. They can reach the hut before evening.

passages.label: C
passages.text: The second day is longer. Walkers take a path 17.5 kilometres up the Clinton Valley. They follow the river and pass a waterfall before reaching Lake Mintaro. From the lake they can see the mountain route ahead. It is the next change in the scenery, after a day in the forest.

passages.label: D
passages.text: On day three, walkers climb to Mackinnon Pass, 1,154 metres high. A shelter stands at the highest point. The view takes in steep cliffs and the valley below. The path then goes down past falls. A side trip leads to Sutherland Falls, which drops 580 metres in three parts.

passages.label: E
passages.text: On the final day, the route passes Mackay Falls, Bell Rock and Lake Ada before reaching Sandfly Point. A short boat ride takes each tourist to Milford Sound. Days of walking give a very different view from the view at the start. Before setting out, ask for directions to the boat and check the location of the car park and toilets. Buy food at a supermarket and allow time for traffic when you arrive.

R_H2.passageTitle: Getting ready for the Milford Track

passages.label: A
passages.text: A map of the Milford Track on New Zealand's South Island shows a route from the mountains to the sea. Its cliffs, waterfalls and scenery make it a famous and popular walk. Weather can turn quickly. Before setting off, walkers should check the forecast and track news. Plan the boat and road trips needed at each end.

passages.label: B
passages.text: A backpack of 40 to 60 litres is useful for this four-day journey. The list issued by the people in charge includes a sleeping bag, a first aid kit, a torch, spare batteries and a rubbish bag. A tourist should also carry details of the booking and identification, and these items help when the path through a forest or valley is dark or wet.

passages.label: C
passages.text: A view of a hill under a blue sky can change in minutes. Rain can move across the valley. Walkers need firm boots they have already worn, a warm top and clothing that keeps rain off. Bring a hat and gloves and keep one dry set of clothes for night. Think about how the same clothes will work in the forest and by a cold river.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Walkers carry every meal and some spare food, since nothing can be bought on the track, and a supermarket can supply quick-cooking food before departure. Confirm the location of the boat, directions to its car park and who to contact if a travel problem arises. When you arrive, follow local advice about getting water from a lake or stream.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Three huts stand along the route, and camping is not permitted. The huts provide bunks, mattresses, heating, toilets, basic cooking places, lights and cold water. A ranger stays at each hut in the main season. The huts do not provide showers or cooking tools. During the Great Walks season, the huts must be booked early. Allow time for traffic when travelling to the park. Good preparation lets walkers enjoy the view over the valley.

R_H3.passageTitle: Life and work across the Maldives

passages.label: A
passages.text: A map of the Maldives shows many islands in the Indian Ocean. Their land is small, but sea separates one island from the next. Malé, the capital, is one place where people change boats or take a small aircraft. An international airport connects the country with visitors from far away.

passages.label: B
passages.text: A map of Malé, the capital, may show the location of a museum, a hospital, a bank and a supermarket before you arrive. If you ask for directions on a busy street, a local person may also point out the traffic at that time of day. A home island with a park or playground can still be very far from a place for serious medical care. That is why many people use boats or other services to travel between islands.

passages.label: C
passages.text: The Maldives is famous for its beach scenery, and a tourist can stay on a resort island or in a guesthouse in a local community. A room with a sea view is part of what some guests come to enjoy. Tourism is also an industry that provides work in hotels, on boats and in food services.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Fishing is another important industry. Tuna has long supported families and communities. Pole-and-line fishing is a traditional method that catches fish one at a time. Workers also prepare fish for food and export. Fishing and tourism both depend on a healthy ocean, so care for marine life supports work as well as nature.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Fishing trips are popular, but rules and activities differ by island. Some visitors spend time on beaches, while others choose a market or an island street. Space for a farm or field is limited on many small islands. The journey between places shows why sea travel and the jobs connected to water are still an important part of this modern country.
